records.old: Part A — Paired Systematic Configuration Practice (25 min): Pairs receive a laminated 'Configuration Table' worksheet listing all 20 elements with atomic number, a blank 'Configuration' column, and a blank 'Outermost Subshell' column. Using the Aufbau diagonal diagram from Lesson 7 (posted on the board), pairs collaboratively write the full s and p configuration for every element H through Ca, then circle the outermost subshell. They then colour-code: red for s-block outer electrons, blue for p-block outer electrons. Part B — Colour-Coded Group Pattern Discovery (10 min): Pairs shade the cells for all Group 1 elements (H, Li, Na, K) in one colour, Group 2 (Be, Mg, Ca) in a second, and the halogens (F, Cl) in a third. They answer two guided questions on the worksheet: (1) 'What do all Group 1 elements have in common in their configuration?' (2) 'How many electrons does each Group 1 element have in its outermost s orbital?' Part C — Reference Check (5 min)

records.old: potassium permanganate solution — a soft violet-lilac colour appears.
records.new: potassium chloride solution — a faint lilac-violet colour appears (fainter and shorter-lived than sodium's yellow, so the room is dimmed; any yellow flicker is sodium contamination from the wire).
records.why: Potassium permanganate solution is itself deep violet, so a violet flame from it would suggest that the flame takes its colour from the solution, which is exactly the idea this lesson wants students to question. Permanganate is also a strong oxidiser and puts manganese into the flame. Potassium chloride solution is colourless, so a lilac flame can only come from potassium; it is the standard flame-test compound and is cheap (sold as a salt substitute or fertiliser). Checked: KMnO4 contains potassium, but flame tests use colourless salts so the solution colour cannot confuse the result. Teacher decides: confirm potassium chloride is obtainable (a wood-ash solution is an alternative) and check the 'Observe' wording against the lilac you actually see.
records.reference: Royal Society of Chemistry (Education), practical 'Flame tests' (testing for metal ions); CLEAPSS student safety sheets for potassium permanganate and potassium chloride
records.group_headline: Potassium was tested with potassium permanganate, whose own violet solution could mislead students; every mention now uses potassium chloride (colourless solution)

records.old: 0.1 M potassium permanganate, and 0.1 M copper sulphate — all low-hazard at these concentrations but must not be ingested.
records.new: 0.1 M potassium chloride, and 0.1 M copper sulphate — all low-hazard at these concentrations but must not be ingested. The wire-cleaning acid is dilute hydrochloric acid (1 M or weaker): teacher only, with goggles and gloves, bottle kept away from the flame, spills rinsed with plenty of water. If there is no nichrome wire or Bunsen burner, soak wooden splints in each solution for about 10 minutes and hold them at the edge of a spirit lamp or candle flame, or put a pinch of each salt on a tin lid with a few drops (no more than 2 mL) of methylated spirit and light it with a taper (teacher only, one sample at a time, spirit bottle closed and well away).
records.why: Follows the potassium chloride change. The notes also never mentioned the hydrochloric acid used to clean the wire, and gave no low-cost option for schools without nichrome wire or Bunsen burners (guideline 8). Splint and methylated-spirit flame tests are standard school alternatives.

records.old: • Carbon-14 Dating of Ancient Kenyan Artefacts: Archaeologists at sites like Olorgesailie use carbon-14 (an isotope of carbon-12) to date ancient tools — students find it puzzling that two atoms of the same element (carbon) can have different masses and different stabilities
records.new: • Dating Ancient Kenyan Artefacts with Radioactive Isotopes: Archaeologists at Olorgesailie date the volcanic ash layers around stone tools hundreds of thousands to over a million years old using potassium-40, a radioactive isotope of potassium; younger remains such as charcoal or bone (less than about 50,000 years old) are dated with carbon-14, an isotope of carbon — students find it puzzling that two atoms of the same element (potassium, or carbon) can have different masses and different stabilities
records.why: Olorgesailie's stone tools are far too old for carbon-14: it has a half-life of 5,730 years and can only date material up to about 50,000 years old. The site is dated from volcanic ash with potassium-argon / argon-argon methods, which use potassium-40 (half-life about 1.25 billion years). Checked by recomputing: 50,000 / 5,730 is about 8.7 half-lives, about 0.2% of carbon-14 left, the practical limit; tools of 500,000+ years would have none. Potassium-40 also links the context to the potassium in the anchoring phenomenon. Teacher decides: name a Kenyan site with younger remains (under 50,000 years) for the carbon-14 example if you wish.
records.reference: National Museums of Kenya, Olorgesailie Prehistoric Site; Potts et al. 2018, Science (Olorgesailie Basin, argon-dated volcanic layers); OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 21 (Nuclear Chemistry), radioactive dating
records.group_headline: Lesson 4 and the unit said Olorgesailie tools are dated by carbon-14, but they are far too old for it; the context now uses potassium-40 for Olorgesailie and carbon-14 for younger remains

records.new: Sodium-23 is stable; sodium-24 is radioactive (half-life about 15 hours) and has been used as a medical tracer. Do they give the same flame colour? Prove it using atomic number.' After 7 minutes, cold-call one group to share their isotope families. Correct any misclassification immediately with: 'Remember — same element means same number of protons. Check atomic number Z first, always.' Teacher note: in a real school flame test the yellow comes from sodium, and chlorine gives no characteristic flame colour, so the Cl-35 / Cl-37 question is about the principle that mass number does not change electron arrangement; if students want to test it, use Na-23 and Na-24 or K-39 and K-41 as the thought experiment.

records.old: rather than explaining them as random scatter.
records.new: rather than explaining them as random scatter. Expected answers for the Explanation Frame: (1) most alpha particles passed straight through because the atom is mostly empty space; (2) a few were deflected at large angles because the positive alpha particles were repelled by a very small, dense, positively charged centre (the nucleus); (3) the atom must be mostly empty space, with a tiny, dense nucleus at its centre. If a group says the particles 'bounced off the electrons', explain that an alpha particle is about 7,300 times heavier than an electron, so electrons cannot turn it back.
records.why: Gives the teacher what a good answer sounds like and the likeliest misconception. Checked: alpha particle mass 6.64 x 10^-27 kg divided by electron mass 9.11 x 10^-31 kg is about 7,290, so about 7,300.
records.reference: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 2 (Atoms, Molecules, and Ions)

records.new: Each pair receives 24 cards (or views them on the ARES tablet) organised in four sets of six, one card per sub-shell: SET A — Sub-shell names (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s); SET B — Shapes (sphere, sphere, three dumbbells, sphere, three dumbbells, sphere); SET C — Principal Energy Level (1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4); SET D — Maximum electrons in the whole sub-shell (2, 2, 6, 2, 6, 2). records.why: The card sort said '20 cards' but listed 9 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 19, had 9 name cards against only 4 shape cards, listed 3px/3py/3pz with only one dumbbell set, and said every orbital holds 2 electrons although the lesson's own table says 2p holds 6. Nothing taught that 4s fills after 3p, yet potassium (19 electrons) must put its last electron in 4s. Rebuilt as one card per sub-shell: 6 x 4 = 24 cards; capacities 2, 2, 6, 2, 6, 2 add to 20 (Ca). Checked: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 = 20 electrons.
records.reference: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 6 (Electronic Structure and Periodic Properties of Elements) (electronic structure of atoms, electron configurations)

records.old: explaining why sodium's 3s→2p transition always gives the same yellow colour
records.new: explaining why sodium's 3p→3s transition (the lone 3s electron is excited to 3p and falls back) always gives the same yellow colour
records.why: A 3s to 2p transition would be a fall to a level that is already full in sodium (2p6) and is not the yellow line. Sodium's yellow doublet (589.0 and 589.6 nm) is the 3p to 3s transition. Checked: E = hc / lambda = (6.626 x 10^-34 J s x 2.998 x 10^8 m/s) / 589 x 10^-9 m = 3.37 x 10^-19 J (about 2.1 eV), the 3s-3p gap used in Lesson 6. Lessons 3-9 say 'jumps up, falls back to 3s', which stays correct.
records.reference: NIST Atomic Spectra Database, sodium (Na I) 589 nm D lines; OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 6 (Electronic Structure and Periodic Properties of Elements)
records.group_headline: The storyline said sodium's yellow comes from a 3s to 2p drop; sodium's yellow light is the 3p to 3s drop, now stated in Lesson 7 and in the Final Explanation exemplar

records.why: Gives teachers the precise transition behind the 'up and back' story (see group headline).
records.reference: NIST Atomic Spectra Database, sodium (Na I)

records.old: with a maximum of 2 electrons in shell 1 and 8 in shell 2, and they cannot exist between shells. Step 1: the flame supplies heat energy. Step 2: the outermost electron in shell 3 absorbs this energy and jumps to a higher energy level. This is the excited state. Step 3: the excited state is unstable, so the electron falls back down to a lower energy level. Step 4: the energy released in the fall is given out as a photon of light. The colour of the light depends on the exact amount of energy released, which depends on the gap between the two energy levels involved in the fall. For sodium, the fall that gives the strong yellow-orange line is from the excited level back to the level of the outermost electron, and its energy gap corresponds to light of about 589 nm. Potassium atoms have a different electron arrangement and differently spaced energy levels
records.new: with a maximum of 2 electrons in shell 1, 8 in shell 2 and 8 in shell 3 (for the first 20 elements), and they cannot exist between shells. Step 1: the flame supplies heat energy. Step 2: the outermost electron in shell 3 absorbs this energy and jumps to a higher energy level. This is the excited state. Step 3: the excited state is unstable, so the electron falls back down to a lower energy level. Step 4: the energy released in the fall is given out as a photon of light. The colour of the light depends on the exact amount of energy released, which depends on the gap between the two energy levels involved in the fall. For sodium, the fall that gives the strong yellow-orange line is from the excited level (in the orbital model, 3p) back to the level the outermost electron started in (3s), and its energy gap corresponds to light of about 589 nm. Potassium (atomic number 19, arrangement 2, 8, 8, 1) has its outermost electron in shell 4 and differently spaced energy levels
records.why: Answers the audit finding on Part 2: the exemplar was vague about which level the electron falls to and gave no shell-3 capacity or potassium arrangement. Checked: 2 + 8 + 8 + 1 = 19.
records.reference: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 6 (Electronic Structure and Periodic Properties of Elements)
records.where: Final Explanation, Part 2: Energy Levels and the Origin of Flame Colour, exemplar

records.new: why do Group 1 metals (Li, Na, K) have the same outer-electron pattern, yet each gives its own flame colour? Students leave ready for Lesson 9, where they will use these configurations to complete their explanatory models of the Kenyan cooking-hearth phenomenon.
records.why: Two problems. Sodium (yellow), potassium (violet) and lithium (crimson) are not 'warm-toned' or 'similar': violet is not a warm colour, and the lesson's own point is that the same outer-electron pattern gives different colours. Also, Lesson 9 is the final model and Driving Question Board lesson, not periodic trends (those belong to Sub-Strand 1.3, The Periodic Table), so Lesson 8 promised content Lesson 9 does not teach.
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Chemistry, Sub-Strand 1.2 The Atom and Sub-Strand 1.3 The Periodic Table; OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 6 (Electronic Structure and Periodic Properties of Elements)

records.old: Part A — Peer-Teaching Carousel (15 min): Each pair is assigned one element from a set of 10 'focus elements' (Ne, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar, Ca). They have 3 minutes to rehearse explaining: (a) the full configuration, (b) how many electrons are in each subshell, and (c) which group the element belongs to and why. Pairs then rotate in a carousel: each pair stands at a station (desk with the element name card) and explains their element to the visiting pair. Visiting pairs must ask at least one question. After 6 minutes, pairs rotate once more.

records.old: Groups then deliver 3-minute gallery-walk presentations, after which the whole class reunites to compose a collective written answer to the driving question on the board. Finally, the teacher leads a structured DQB closure: students vote on which wonder questions are now fully answered, which are partially answered, and which are passed forward to Sub-Strand 1.3. The lesson ends with individual exit slips that serve as the summative formative checkpoint for the sub-strand.
records.new: Groups then present in a two-round gallery walk (about 2 minutes per visiting group), after which the whole class reunites to compose a collective written answer to the driving question on the board. Finally, the teacher leads a structured DQB closure: students vote on which wonder questions are now fully answered, which are partially answered, and which are passed forward to Sub-Strand 1.3. The lesson ends with individual exit slips that serve as the summative formative checkpoint for the sub-strand. Suggested timing for the 80 minutes: Predict 8, Observe 10, Explain 40 (25 build, 12 gallery walk, 3 class answer), Driving Question Board 12, exit slip 10.
records.why: Groups of 4-5 in a class of 40-50 means 8-12 groups; 3 minutes each is 24-36 minutes, but the plan gives the gallery walk 12. Running it in two rounds (half the groups present while the others visit, then swap) fits 12 minutes. Minutes now add up: 8 + 10 + 40 + 12 + 10 = 80.

value.criterion: Use of evidence from the lessons
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: uses specific evidence from several lessons, such as the flame test colours, gold foil results, Bohr diagrams, orbital configurations and the chlorine data, and links each piece to the explanation.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: uses some evidence from the lessons, but the link to the explanation is sometimes missing or general.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: gives little evidence, or states facts without any link to the lessons.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: correctly sequences absorption of energy, jump to the excited state, fall to a lower level and emission of a photon, and explains that the colour depends on the energy gap, which is unique to each element.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: describes the jump and the release of light but is vague about why the colour is specific to the element.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: describes the flame colour without a correct explanation of electron jumps or energy release.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: writes correct configurations for sodium and potassium, applies the Aufbau, Pauli and Hund rules, and explains how 3s¹ versus 4s¹ leads to different colours.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: writes mostly correct configurations and states the rules, with limited link to the colours.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: configurations are incomplete or partly incorrect, and the rules are confused.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: calculates 35.5 correctly with a reasonableness check and explains that isotopes share electron arrangement and so the same flame colour.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: calculates correctly but gives an incomplete explanation of the flame colour of isotopes.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: the calculation is incorrect or the idea of isotopes is confused.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: uses precise vocabulary (nucleus, shell, orbital, excited state, photon), a logical order and the Kenyan context throughout.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: uses mostly correct vocabulary and a clear order, with minor errors.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: uses little scientific vocabulary and the ideas are hard to follow.

records.why: The contract has three level fields (excellent, proficient, developing) that print under fixed headings, so the level names Exceeds, Meets and Approaches Expectations now start each descriptor. The wording is otherwise unchanged except 'incomplete or partly incorrect' for the lowest configuration level, so 'Approaches' does not describe a missing answer.
